lines.text: Your project builds, and there's nothing in it yet. The first class you write by hand is one physical part of the robot. We'll follow the arm.
Where the file lands matters. The new folder has to sit right beside the robot class, and one made a level up puts your code in the wrong package.
You start from a template, and most of its imports will be greyed out. That's fine. They wake up as you fill the class in.
The fields are the hardware you already met in Tuner X: the bus, the motor, and the CANcoder. If your bench came out with different numbers, change the code to match.
Watch the bus name. It has to be spelled the way you named it in Tuner X, or nothing answers.
You don't type the configuration. Tuner X already has it, so it writes the code and you paste that into the constructor.
The config printed on the page is ours, there for its shape. Paste your own over the whole thing, and if your gains come along, leave them in.
For the arm, one part of that config matters most. The motor's own count starts from zero at every power-on, so the config points it at the absolute encoder instead.
Two short methods finish the class. One sets the number on the request you built as a field and sends it. The other stops the motor, and Coast takes over.
Plain voltage is only a simple test. This table is the rest of the family, and the one you finished Workshop 1 on drops in just as easily.
A motor keeps applying the last request it got, even after the code that sent it has stopped running. That's what the stop method is for.
The robot class gets one field for the arm. It's public, so every OpMode you write later can reach it.
Nothing here moves a motor, so the check is a clean build. Both methods are still private and nothing calls them, and turning them into commands is the next lesson.
